opus-5.5.text:
I think the missing piece is the specification. For decades, formal verification has had a reputation of being beautiful but impractical. People built incredible tools: proof assistants like Lean, Coq, Isabelle, model checkers, SMT solvers. And there are real success stories, like verified compilers, verified microkernels, and parts of cryptographic libraries. But each of those took enormous human effort, often many person-years of PhD-level work, to verify a relatively small amount of code.

So the bottleneck has been twofold. First, writing the proofs is extremely labor-intensive. Second, and I think more fundamentally, someone has to write down precisely what the software is supposed to do. That is the specification, and it is often harder than writing the code itself. Most engineers have never been trained to think that way, and in the real world requirements are fuzzy, they change, and they live in people's heads or in a Slack thread.

What has changed is AI. Models are getting very good at generating code, which means we will soon have far more code than humans can ever review. That makes the trust problem much more urgent. If an AI writes a million lines, how do you know it is correct? Testing only samples behavior. Code review doesn't scale. A formal proof is the only thing that gives you a guarantee about all possible inputs.

The opportunity is that the same AI advances can attack both bottlenecks. On the proof side, we're already seeing systems that can generate proofs in Lean at a level that was unthinkable a few years ago, partly because math is such a clean training ground: the checker tells you right or wrong, and there's no reward hacking. On the specification side, AI can help translate informal intent into formal statements, and then a human only needs to review the spec, which is much shorter and more readable than the code or the proof.

So the vision I find compelling is that you separate concerns. The human says what they want. The AI writes the code and the proof. And a small, trusted kernel checks that the proof is valid. You don't have to trust the AI at all; you only have to trust the checker and your own reading of the specification.

That's why I think mathematics and software verification are really the same problem viewed from two angles. If you can build an AI that reasons rigorously in mathematics, proving theorems in a formal language, you have essentially built the engine for verified software. The missing piece is bringing that engine together with good specification tools and making it cheap enough that verification becomes the default, not a luxury reserved for aerospace or chip design.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly names the specification as the missing piece and says precisely stating what software should do is a fundamental bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It describes AI proving theorems in formal languages and connecting mathematical reasoning to software verification, but does not express the aspiration that every problem that can be formulated mathematically will be proved.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the missing piece is honestly not a technical gap in the sense of needing a new theorem or a new proof technique. The missing piece is making verification something a working engineer can actually use without having to become a specialist in it.

If you look at where formal methods stand today, the tools are powerful. Lean, Coq, Isabelle, SMT solvers, model checkers. You can prove remarkably deep properties about systems. But the cost is enormous. A verified compiler or a verified kernel takes years of effort by a small team of people who have spent a decade learning the craft. Most companies simply cannot afford that, so verification stays at the margins, in aerospace, in some parts of hardware, in a few critical security components. The vast majority of software in the world that actually runs our lives has never been formally verified and probably never would be under the old economics.

So the thing I keep coming back to is that specification and proof have historically been bottlenecked on human labor. You need someone to write down precisely what the program is supposed to do, which is often harder than writing the program itself, and then you need someone to produce a proof that the implementation matches that specification. Both of those steps have been manual, slow, and fragile. Change one line of code and the proof breaks and you have to go back and repair it.

What I think is changing, and what we are working on, is that AI can now take over a huge share of that labor. Large models are getting genuinely good at generating candidate proofs, at suggesting invariants, at translating informal intent into formal statements. And the beautiful thing about pairing AI with formal verification is that the two cover each other's weaknesses. The model can be creative and fast but it hallucinates. The proof checker is slow to write for by hand but it never lies. If a model produces a proof and the checker accepts it, you do not have to trust the model at all. The kernel of the proof assistant is the source of truth.

So for me the missing piece is that closed loop. An AI system that proposes, a verifier that judges, and the feedback from the verifier flowing back to make the next proposal better. Once you have that, verification stops being an artisanal activity and starts being something that scales with compute rather than with the number of PhDs you can hire.

There is still a hard problem underneath, which is specification. Even if proofs become cheap, you still need to say what correct means, and for a lot of real software people genuinely do not know until they see it fail. I think AI can help there too, by proposing specifications and letting humans refine them, but I would say that is where the frontier will sit for a while. The proof side is becoming tractable. The specification side is where the deep questions remain.

r001.rationale: The response says the specification side is where the deep questions remain, while the proof side is becoming tractable, identifying specification as the current bottleneck.

r002.rationale: The response describes making verification scale through AI and compute, but does not state an aspiration to prove every problem that can be formulated mathematically.

astra-6.text:
I think the missing piece is making verification practical for the people writing software. Testing tells you that your code works on the cases you tried. Verification asks whether it satisfies a specification across all the cases that specification covers. But that requires you to express what you want precisely and then connect that specification to the implementation.

So there are really two challenges: making proofs easier to produce, and making sure we’re proving the right thing. AI could help with the first by generating specifications and proofs, with a verifier checking the proofs. But the second still requires understanding the developer’s intent. A proof can be correct while the specification misses something important.

r001.rationale: The response describes expressing intent as one challenge, alongside making proofs easier, but does not identify specification as the current bottleneck.

r002.rationale: The response discusses proofs checked by a verifier but does not express the aspiration to prove any problem that can be formulated mathematically.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the missing piece is connecting what we can prove about software to what we actually want it to do. A proof can establish that a program satisfies a specification, but that leaves a crucial question: did we write the right specification?

That’s where human intent still matters enormously. We need tools that help developers express their assumptions, identify ambiguous requirements, and understand exactly what a proof guarantees. Automating proofs is valuable, but making those proofs meaningful—and practical enough to use throughout development—is the bigger challenge.

r001.rationale: It says a proof can satisfy a specification while the crucial question is whether the specification is right, identifying specification as the missing piece.

r002.rationale: It calls proof automation valuable but does not express the aspiration to prove every problem that can be formulated mathematically.
